ABSENT: None. ALSO PRESENT: Kenneth Young, City Manager (Zoom); Michelle Bailey Hedgepeth, Deputy City Manager; Yvette Allen, City Clerk; Stephanie Anderson, City Attorney; Kiaisha Barber, Director of Youth, Family and Senior Services; Miriam Barber, Director of Planning, Moira Abernethy, Executive Assistant; Michael Williams, Director of Economic Development; Emma Martin, Student Liaison and Sammi Saeed, Deputy Student Liaison. Mayor Kabir opened the meeting at 7:30 p.m. AMENDMENTS TO AND APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA A motion was made by Mayor Pro Tem Mitchell and seconded by Councilmember Mitchell to amend the agenda by removing Worksession Item D, Overview and Research on Scooters, E-Bikes, and E-Motos, from the agenda. The motion passed 8-0-0. A motion was made by Councilmember Mitchell and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mackie to approve the agenda as amended. The motion passed 8-0-0. PUBLIC COMMENT Alexandra (Sasha) Tyukavina, resident, asked the Council to light City playgrounds so they can remain open after dark, starting with the new Duvall Field playground. She said the walkways, pickleball courts, and soccer fields are lit, while police enforce the playground's after-dark closure. She noted that daylight is shrinking and that many families use the playground between 6:00 and 8:00 p.m. She suggested adding a single LED streetlight to the existing utility pole at the southeastern corner. She also suggested redirecting funds from the $30,000 public safety study toward public space safety features, and she asked that the topic be added to a future work session. Mayor Kabir agreed the points were well taken. Mark Srour, owner of Cornerstone Grill, and Brian Lambert, its general manager, asked the 018 Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes October 20, 2026 Page 2 Council to support reducing a three-month suspension proposed by the liquor board. They said the closure would cost 70 employees their jobs, many of them students. Councilmember Hernandez asked whether the rules could be suspended to follow up. Councilmember Mitchell said the sensitivity of the matter made it inappropriate for open discussion. She recommended reaching out to the parties involved for the report and bringing it back through the District 3 councilmembers. Mayor Kabir directed staff to work with the District 3 councilmembers. Mr. Srour noted that his attorney is Linda Carter. Arelis Prez, resident, expressed her strong opposition to removing scheduled agenda items from the agenda without providing the public with adequate advance notice or a clear explanation of why the item is being removed from the agenda. WORKSESSION ITEMS: Education and Literacy Overview Director of Youth, Family and Senior Services Kiaisha Barber, Education Consultants Melinda Coles and Vincent Johns presented updates on six education initiatives. Tutoring and Imagine Learning: Staff reported that the $30,000 Imagine Learning contract expires at the end of the following week. Of the 68 registered profiles, none had completed a learning module. Staff recommended discontinuing the service and promoting the free Brainfuse resource. They also recommended reallocating the funds to school-based tutoring, the Latino Student Fund STEM Saturday program, and expanded elementary tutoring support through programs such as Amplify. Public School Education Grant Eligibility: Staff proposed revised grant categories and application materials for implementation during the current fiscal year. They also noted that the existing funding tiers do not adequately account for non-boundary schools with significant College Park student enrollment. Summer Camp Scholarships: Staff proposed adding a financial need requirement, providing a hardship application process, and releasing scholarship applications in January. Family Education and Resource Navigation: Staff recommended leveraging existing Prince George's County Public Schools (PGCPS) resources and exploring the creation of an Education Liaison position. Adult ESL: Staff recommended partnering with existing college and community-based providers to expand adult English as a Second Language opportunities. PGCPS Volunteer Registration: Staff proposed hosting a standalone mobile fingerprinting event at a cost of $60 per person, with a minimum of 15 participants and a total minimum cost of $900. 019 Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes October 20, 2026 Page 3 Ms. Barber explained that the $40,000 consultant budget supports up to 20 hours of work per week. Mr. Johns noted that PGCPS's countywide organizational structure can make it challenging for municipalities to influence school system priorities. During Council discussion, Councilmembers Mitchell, Ranker, Hernandez, Hew, Oates, Jordan, and Mayor Pro Tem Mackie, supported discontinuing Imagine Learning due to its limited use. Councilmembers Hew and Hernandez, and Mayor Pro Tem Mackie, praised the Amplify tutoring program and supported expanding its availability. Councilmember Ranker emphasized the importance of strategic stewardship and providing comprehensive support services rather than simply reallocating the $30,000 in funding. He also recommended informing schools that continued funding is not guaranteed for the next fiscal year. Councilmember Hernandez supported distributing funds to schools based on their individual strategic needs and encouraged building long-term relationships with schools and supporting parent-teacher organizations. Waiver Request – 611 Holdings II Storage Yard Mr. Bruce Howe of Vista Design and Mr. Mark Spencer Cropper, the applicant’s attorney, approached the table. Mr. Howe provided a brief overview of the project and summarized the requests being made. Two waivers were requested: one from the paving requirements to allow gravel within the storage yard, and another from the screening requirements to allow a chainlink fence with privacy slats to be used in lieu of landscaping. Mr. Cropper gave a brief history of the project’s proceedings with the Board of Appeals, noting that multiple variances and special exceptions were previously granted for the use of the property as a storage yard, the installation of a privacy fence, and relief from the front-yard setback requirements. Following a brief discussion, Mr. French noted that he believes a fence with privacy slats by itself does not fit the neighborhood and believes the applicant should move forward with landscaped screening or possibly a more aesthetically pleasing fence material. Other members of the commission concurred. Steve Engel from Vista Design approached the table. He mentioned concerns about the landscaping being destroyed when SHA does maintenance and mows the lawns along the highways. Mr. Barbierri found it necessary to move forward with the gravel waiver request before continuing the discussion about the landscaping waiver. The Commission moved to grant the waiver request for the application of gravel on the lot motioned by Mrs. Ott and seconded by Mr. French, and the motion was approved unanimously. Further discussion regarding the landscaped screening waiver continued. Following this, Mr. Cropper decided to withdraw the waiver from the landscaping, and discuss steps to move forward with the applicant with plans to return at a later date. IV. Waiver Request –10529 Flower St / Build Pines LLC– Contractor Shops Hugh Cropper, attorney for Build Pines LLC, and Ben Sharp, owner of Build Pines LLC, approached the table. Mr. Cropper provided a brief overview of the project and its location. Two waivers were requested: a waiver from the paving requirements to allow gravel in the driving and parking areas, and a waiver from the screening requirements, as the proposed buildings will be screened from view by existing forest After some brief discussion Mr. French motioned to approval the waiver for the landscaping screening requirements, seconded by Mrs. Wimbrow and the motion was approved unanimously. Page 2 of 5 WORCESTER COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES – October 1, 2026 Mr. Barbierri prompted the commissioners for questions or comments regarding the waiver for the gravel. After a couple of brief questions and answers, Mrs. Wimbrow motioned to approved the waiver, seconded by Mrs. Ott and the motion was approved unanimously. V. Atlantic Coastal Bays Growth Allocation Request – Salt Life Park (Phase 3) Mr. Hugh Cropper, attorney, Chris McCabe, Coastal Compliance Solutions LLC, Steve Engel, Vista Design Inc., and Mark Odachowski, owner of Salt Life Phase III approached the table. Mr. Cropper gave an overview of the existing Salt Life Community and provided a history of the property for which the growth allocation requested. He then provided background on the Coastal Bays Critical Area program and growth allocation requests in general. Mr. Cropper also explained the standards for growth allocation in the Critical Area law as well as the new standards related to environmental justice and resiliency. Mr. Cropper questioned Mr. Engel to confirm that the growth allocation request meets the standards in the Critical Area law. Mr. Engel confirmed that the request meets or exceeds the standards. Mr. Cropper questioned Mr. Odachowski about the economic benefit that the existing Salt Life Community has had in the area. Mr. Odachowski stated he believes there has been a positive economic impact. Mr. Cropper questioned Mr. McCabe on the environmental impacts associated with the proposed growth allocation. Mr. McCabe confirmed that the environmental impacts were minimal and all required mitigation and stormwater requirements would be met. Mr. Cropper finished his presentation by stating the growth allocation request and proposed development are good examples of infill development and an appropriate use of the County’s allotted growth allocation acreage. Mr. Barbierri asked Mr. McCabe to explain the new standards of environmental justice and resilience. Mr. McCabe stated that the only metric that exceeded the threshold for environmental justice was low birth rate. He explained how the developer worked with Worcester County Parks and Recreation to perform the mitigation at Homer Gudelsky Park and the Herring Creek Nature Park benefiting residents. Mrs. Phyllis Wimbrow asked if the owner was aware growth allocation would be needed when the zoning map amendment was approved in 2025. Mr. Cropper replied that the Critical Area designation was discussed by the Planning Commission and County Commissioners at their respective meetings. Mr. Alec French asked if the owner was aware of the Critical Area and zoning regulations, specifically the density, when he purchased the property. Mr. Odachowski and Mr. Cropper stated the property was purchased in 1999 prior to the existence of the Atlantic Coastal Bays Critical Area. Page 3 of 5 WORCESTER COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES – October 1, 2026 Mr. Cropper explained how growth allocation is calculated and how the allocation is awarded. Mr. Brian Soper stated there will be 360 acres of growth allocation for the coastal bays remaining if this request is approved. Mr. French voiced his concerns about the environmental impacts of the growth allocation and the development associated with it. Mr. Cropper explained how the proposed development meets all the standards of growth allocation and the intent of the comprehensive plan. Mrs. Wimbrow stated she shared the concerns of Mr. French however she explained how the proposed development is consistent with the comprehensive plan and zoning in addition to bringing affordable housing to the area. A motion was made by Mrs. Marlene Ott to forward a favorable recommendation. The motion was seconded by Mrs. Wimbrow, and the motion was approved 5-1 with Mr. French opposing. VI. Text Amendment - §Z 1-303 CA Commercial Airport District Zachary Williams, Venable, attorney for the applicants; Rob Corradi and Ellis Harkins, Amazon, applicants; Jeremey Sweeny, applicant, Maryland Broadband Cooperative (MdBC) board member; and Drew Van Dopp, CEO MdBC, were present for the review. Mr. Corradi explained that the text amendment concerns a power feed equipment (PFE) building, not a cable landing station (CLS) or data center, which are subject to the moratorium. The proposal is for one 1,200-square-foot building on a 3,500-square-foot site at the airport. The building would not connect to public water or sewer and is being developed with the Maryland Broadband Cooperative (MdBC). Mr. Williams said the applicants had provided an additional letter addressing public comments and expected to answer questions about the project. The Planning Commission asked about Globalinx’s involvement, lease agreements between Amazon and Ocean City, and contracts between Amazon and MdBC. The applicants clarified that the building’s size and power limits would allow it to serve only one subsea cable. It would boost fiber-optic signals between the subsea cable, overseas connections, and fiber lines to the Washington area. They stated that no CLS or data center is planned for Worcester County. Cable manufacturing is beginning, with installation anticipated in late 2027, pending required permits and approvals. Commission members asked about the cable’s right-of-way, potential conflicts with other utilities, and local benefits. The applicants said they are working with MdBC to connect the cable to Washington and that it would expand broadband capacity without requiring local funding. Mr. Van Dopp explained that the project could create more reliable fiber pathways, Page 4 of 5 WORCESTER COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES – October 1, 2026 reduce service bottlenecks on the Eastern Shore, and benefit highways, schools, health care providers, and local businesses. Further discussion focused on the project’s technical requirements, community benefits, and costs. Although the proposed building appeared limited in scope, commissioners recognized that the application is very technical and could have significant community impacts. The Planning Commission confirmed that staff could not reject the application. However, because the zoning code requires a recommendation only “within a reasonable time,” it does not establish a specific deadline. Ms. Wimbrow moved to postpone consideration of the text amendment for 60 days to allow additional study. Ms. Drew seconded the motion, which passed unanimously, with Mr. Barbierri, Mr. French, Ms. Purnell-Milbourne, and Ms. Ott voting in favor. Next step: The Planning Commission will revisit the text amendment request at a future meeting, no sooner than December 2026. VII. text: Public Comment Tuesday, November 3, 2026 26-G-100 Traffic Calming Device: Wellesley Drive Sent: Tuesday, October 13, 2026 2:30 PM To: comc <cpmc@collegeparkmd.gov> Subject: Installation of Traffic Calming on Wellesley Drive Dear Mayor and Council of the City of College Park, | live at 7600 Wellesley Drive. | am not in favor of the installation of speed bumps on my road. It does not seem fair to penalize all of the residents on Wellesley for the act of a few errant drivers. Your survey report does not state the type of vehicles in violation but | have observed many one-offs in a hurry; that is delivery trucks and vehicles that are non-residential. The speed bumps and stop signs installed on Old Calvert Road are excessive and | would challenge any driver to risk damage to their vehicle by transversing this road at or below the posted speed limit. | do not want to see this happen on Wellesley Drive. | would be in favor of temporary speed cameras set up to warn people that speeding thru my neighborhood comes with consequences. Also, the residents at 7400 Wellesley do not speak for all the residents of Wellesley despite what was heard at the meeting of the proposed sidewalk. And since this is a council decision, | hold dim hope that dissenting voices will hold weight. Thank you, Sent: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 3:33 PM To: cpmc <cpmc@collegeparkmd.gov> Subject: Pedestrian Safety on St. Andrew's Place Mayor & Council Members, | have lived in College Park Woods on Gettysburg Lane for over 50 years and have witnessed, with great concern, St Andrews Street become increasing more dangerous for pedestrians. With cars parked on both sides of the street, pedestrians are forced to walk in the traffic lanes or trespass on lawns. Staff recommended discontinuing the service and promoting the free Brainfuse resource. They also recommended reallocating the funds to school-based tutoring, the Latino Student Fund STEM Saturday program, and expanded elementary tutoring support through programs such as Amplify. Public School Education Grant Eligibility: Staff proposed revised grant categories and application materials for implementation during the current fiscal year. They also noted that the existing funding tiers do not adequately account for non-boundary schools with significant College Park student enrollment. Summer Camp Scholarships: Staff proposed adding a financial need requirement, providing a hardship application process, and releasing scholarship applications in January. 1 Family Education and Resource Navigation: Staff recommended leveraging existing Prince George's County Public Schools (PGCPS) resources and exploring the creation of an Education Liaison position. Councilmember Ranker emphasized the importance of strategic stewardship and providing comprehensive support services rather than simply reallocating the $30,000 in funding. He also recommended informing schools that continued funding is not guaranteed for the next fiscal year. Councilmember Hernandez supported distributing funds to schools based on their individual strategic needs and encouraged building long-term relationships with schools and supporting parent-teacher organizations. Mayor Pro Tem Mackie also questioned whether parents have sufficient time and resources to participate in the proposed programs. He also noted that non-boundary schools serve approximately one-fifth of College Park students. Councilmember Simmons noted that the current grant program structure may disproportionately benefit schools serving fewer College Park students. Regarding summer camp scholarships, Councilmember Jordan supported requiring a minimum family copayment similar to Montgomery County's 20% requirement. Councilmember Simmons questioned whether additional eligibility restrictions were appropriate for a relatively small program and suggested considering increased funding if the program is oversubscribed. title: Public Work Session Notice
text: PUBLIC WORK SESSION NOTICE The meeting will be held on Thursday, November 12th, 2026 at 3:00 PM at 701 Kelly Rd, Cumberland, MD, 21502 in Room 230. This meeting is open to the media/public for observation and will be streamed on the County website for live viewing and playback. The Allegany County Board of County Commissioners will hold a PUBLIC WORK SESSION to discuss the following: • • Public Business Meeting Agenda Items Department Updates, as needed It is anticipated that the Board of County Commissioners will move to convene a closed session to discuss the following: To discuss public security, if the public body determines that public discussion would constitute a risk to the public or to public security, including the deployment of police services and staff, specifically relating to the purchase of three vehicles by the Allegany County Narcotics Taskforce and one vehicle by the Allegany County Sheriff's Office, all designed to be unmarked and/or undercover vehicles. (General Provisions Article Section 3305 (b)(7)). Persons expected to be present during all or part of the closed session are all three County Commissioners; Jason M. Bennett, County Administrator; T. Lee Beeman, Jr., County Attorney; as well as Recording Secretary, Madison Taylor. A work session is a meeting where the Board of County Commissioners and staff gather to discuss issues, review information, and deliberate on upcoming decisions in a more informal setting than a regular meeting. The purpose of a work session is to allow for indepth discussions, planning, and collaboration without the need for formal votes or public debate. Unlike regular meetings, work sessions typically do not include a public comment period because they are meant for internal discussion and information-gathering rather than decision-making. Since no formal actions are taken, public input is usually reserved for official meetings where votes or policies are considered. However, members of the public are welcome to attend and observe the session.

This event, at once both mellow and exuberant, was enjoyed by dozens of Grovers on a gorgeous Fall Saturday afternoon. • To the group of enterprising volunteers who refurbished “Ann’s Folly” (the tennis shed), which was re-dedicated last Saturday. Included are Anne Vincent, Bob Booher, Bill Robertson, David Stopak, Leigh Partington, Steve Werts, Meredith Horan, Rick Silton, Rod Rivard, Margo Cavenaugh, Bruce Cowie, Dave Cosson, Jim Snyder. Special mention goes to woodworker Terry Arnold, wrangler Meredith Horan and straw boss Bruce Daggy for their contributions to the project. Their skillful restoration has revived and enhanced the artistic decorative features created in 1999 by Jim Fletcher for the building conceived by former Mayor Ann Briggs, built by volunteers, and named to honor Ann’s many contributions to the Grove. • To dedicated Meadows Committee volunteers for planting 350 native wildflowers and grasses on one day and on a second day, the Weed Warrior assault on non-native invasives: Bob & Peggy Booher, Bruce Daggy, Kriss Grisham, Ernie Kawasaki, Paula Puglisi, Kitty Seiferlein, David Stopak, and Anne Vincent. • To the 14(!) Also, within the month, work at the intersection of Hutches Way and Chestnut avenue may resume. The purpose of this public hearing is to take public comment on the rezoning application. REPORT-IN-BRIEF: Application is being made to amend multiple sections of the Forest Conservation Ordinance (FCO) to comply with the requirements of Maryland Senate Bill 256 (SB 256) and to provide clarification of existing regulations currently found in the FCO to meet the intent of Maryland’s Forest Conservation Act (FCA). DISCUSSION: The proposed amendments are primarily mandated by SB 526, passed in 2023. Subsequent amendments under HB1511 required that most changes under the original bill be adopted by counties by July 1, 2026. In addition to the state-mandated changes to the FCO, additional changes have been proposed by staff to text in the Ordinance. These changes are necessary to modernize our Ordinance, as it has never been comprehensively amended since its adoption locally in 1993. This item was presented to the Washington County Planning Commission at a Public Information Meeting held during their regular meeting on June 1, 2026. It was then brought back for recommendation at the July 6, 2026 meeting, where the members unanimously voted in favor of the approval of the proposed amendments. ARTICLE 2 DEFINITIONS In this Ordinance the following terms have the meanings indicated. 2.1 "Afforestation" The establishment of a forest, according to the definitions and procedures contained herein, on an area not presently in forest cover. 2.2. "Agricultural activity" Farming activities, including plowing, tillage, cropping, installation of best management practices, seeding, cultivating, and harvesting for the production of food and fiber products, except commercial logging and timber harvesting operations. This term includes the grazing and raising of livestock, aquaculture, sod production, orchards, nurseries, and other products cultivated as part of a recognized commercial enterprise. 2.3 "Agricultural and resource areas" Undeveloped areas zoned for densities of less than or equal to one dwelling unit per 5 acres and corresponds to Washington County Zoning Classifications A, EC and P. 2.4 "Applicant" A person as defined in Section 2.49 who is applying for subdivision, site plan, grading or sediment control permit approval, or who has received approval of a forest stand delineation or forest conservation plan. 1 2.5 "Approved forest management plan" A document approved by the Department of Natural Resources forester assigned to Washington County which operates as a protective agreement for forest conservation as described in the Natural Resources Article, §5-1607(e)-(f), Annotated Code of Maryland. 2.6 “Best Management Practice (BMP).” Conservation practices or systems of practices and management measures that: A. Control soil loss and reduce water quality degradation caused by nutrients, animal waste, toxics, and sediment; and B. Minimize adverse impacts to the surface water, groundwater flow and circulation patterns, and to their chemical, physical, and biological characteristics. 2.7 "Caliper" The diameter of a tree measured at 2 inches above the root collar. 2.8 "Champion tree" The largest tree of its species within the United States, the State of Maryland, Washington County, or a municipality. 2.9 “C.O.M.A.R.” The Code of Maryland Regulations. Any reference to a specific C.O.M.A.R. section shall include any amendments to that section or any successor sections that may be subsequently adopted. 2.10 "Commercial and industrial uses" Manufacturing operations, office complexes, shopping centers, and other similar uses and their associated storage areas, yarding, and parking areas, and corresponds to the uses enumerated in Washington County Zoning Ordinance classifications BT, BL, BG, HI, ORT, PB, RB, RV, SED, IG, , PI, AP, IM and IR. 2.11 "Commercial logging or timber harvesting operations" The cutting and removing of tree stems from a site for commercial purposes, leaving the root mass intact. The cutting and removal of trees from a site for the purpose of preparing the site for future development is not included in this definition. 2 2.12 "Critical habitat area" A critical habitat for an endangered species and its surrounding protection area. A critical habitat area shall: A. Be likely to contribute to the long-term survival of the species; B. Be likely to be occupied by the species for the foreseeable future; and C. Constitute habitat of the species which is considered critical under Natural Resources Article, §§4-2A-04 and 10-2A-06, Annotated Code of Maryland. 2.13 "Critical habitat for endangered species" A habitat occupied by an endangered species as determined or listed under Natural Resources Article, §§4-2A-04 and 10-2A-04, Annotated Code of Maryland. 2.14 "Declaration of intent" A. Areas that have been cut but not cleared of stumps or the root mat may also be included. "Forest" does not include orchards. 2.22 "Forest Conservancy District Board" The forestry board created for The Washington County Forestry Conservancy District under Natural Resources Article,
